chapters.title: Introduction — One church, many eras
transcript: Welcome to the Collegiate Church of the Most Holy Saviour, in Piazza Roma, at the foot of the castle hill in /A ˈdʒiːra/.
This church holds centuries of religious and artistic history. Its columns, chapels, and artworks reveal different periods in the life of the building and its community.
We will explore its medieval origins, its devotional images, and a precious reminder of the town’s Jewish heritage.
Let us begin outside, before allowing the details within to guide us.

chapters.title: Chapter 1 — The origins of the collegiate church
transcript: The Most Holy Saviour is among the oldest churches in /A ˈdʒiːra/. Its original layout dates back at least to the twelfth century, during the Norman period.
For centuries, its history was linked to the Abbey of San Filippo and Santa Maria Latina in Jerusalem.

The façade, combining late Renaissance design with Baroque elements, took shape mainly in the mid-seventeenth century. The bell tower also preserves traces of rebuilding after the earthquake of sixteen ninety-three.
In sixteen eighty-nine, Francesco Carafa, Bishop of Catania, granted the church collegiate status, establishing a chapter of canons.
The same year appears in an inscription on one of the column capitals.

chapters.title: Chapter 2 — Columns and capitals
transcript: If you can enter, notice the unusual shape of the interior: its ground plan is almost square.
Two rows of columns support the arches and divide the church into a central nave and two side aisles. Above the central nave, you can see the wooden trusses supporting the roof.
Look closely at the capitals, at the tops of the columns.
Each is different. Scrolls, plant motifs, and figures invite you to compare their carved decorations.
Choose one detail, then look for what changes on the next column. It is a simple way to discover the variety within this space.

chapters.title: Chapter 3 — The Chapel of Saint Philip the Deacon
transcript: For centuries, the left aisle belonged to the Abbey and was dedicated to Saint Philip the Deacon, known locally as San Filippu u nicu or San Fulippuzzu.
He is a different figure from Saint Philip of /A ˈdʒiːra/, the town’s patron saint.
In the late sixteenth century, the altar was enriched with an elaborate carved surround.
An old iron gate enclosed the space that housed the chest containing the town’s relics.
Some relics and devotional objects are traditionally associated with the Holy Places of Palestine. These connections form part of the community’s religious memory.

chapters.title: Chapter 4 — The abbots’ treasures
transcript: Among the precious objects associated with the church are a mitre, the ceremonial headdress, and a crozier, the curved staff carried by abbots.
Their origins and dates have been debated over time.
According to studies cited in local historical accounts, the mitre took its present form in the mid-sixteenth century, incorporating older enamels, gems, pearls, and embroidery.
The curved head of the crozier is generally dated to the fourteenth century.
Both reflect the refinement of Sicilian craftsmanship in precious materials. Ask at the church whether they can be viewed during your visit.

chapters.title: Chapter 5 — Images of devotion
transcript: A precious panel painting depicts Saint Philip of /A ˈdʒiːra/ holding a book, with a chained demon beneath his feet.
The image recalls the tradition of the saint as a deliverer from demonic forces.

It is considered a surviving section of a polyptych, an artwork made up of several painted panels. Its artist and date remain uncertain, although a date in the late fourteenth century has been proposed.
In the right aisle, the altar of Our Lady of the Rosary holds an eighteenth-century painting of the Virgin and Dominican saints.
The church is also associated with Easter, when the meeting between the Risen Christ and the Virgin Mary renews a deeply cherished local tradition.

chapters.title: Chapter 6 — The Aron and Jewish memory
transcript: In the left aisle stands the reassembled Aron ha-Qodesh, the ark that once held the Torah scrolls in the old synagogue on Via Santa Croce.
Dating from fourteen fifty-four, it preserves the memory of the medieval Jewish community of /A ˈdʒiːra/.
Carved from stone, it is recognised as one of Europe’s three oldest surviving stone synagogue arks.
Its Hebrew inscription recalled an invitation from the prophet Isaiah to walk in the light of the Lord.

The Aron was not originally part of this church. Following the expulsion of the Jews from Sicily, the synagogue was converted to Christian worship. As that building later deteriorated, the ark was recovered and reassembled here.
You can explore its story further with the dedicated Aron audio guide on Hello /A ˈdʒiːra/.

chapters.title: Closing — Continue exploring
transcript: Our visit ends here.
Before moving on, take another look at a detail that caught your attention: a capital, a chapel, or the stonework of the Aron.
Please respect the spaces used for prayer and check with the church about access to individual artworks.
Continue exploring the historic centre with Hello /A ˈdʒiːra/, a free, independent project created and curated by Giuseppe Ricceri to share and celebrate the town’s heritage.
Thank you for listening, and enjoy discovering /A ˈdʒiːra/!
